policy_label: LightGBM + GRU, whichever is more worried
model_text: Septris combines two models: LightGBM, a decision-tree model that reads hand-made summaries of the last few hours (current values, recent changes, 6-hour highs and lows, which tests were done when); and a GRU, a deep-learning model built by Miheer that reads each patient's hours in order: the hour-by-hour vital signs and lab results, which ones were actually measured, and how long ago each was last measured, plus age and sex. Each model gives every bed a 0-100 risk, and Septris uses the higher of the two, so a bed moves up the line if either model is worried about it. We tried 8 ways of using the two models (each alone, 3 weighted averages, taking the higher of the two, and taking turns), judged only on validation patients, never on the test patients. This 'whichever is more worried' mix came out on top, essentially tied with the GRU alone. The 'what stood out' reasons come from whichever model gave the higher risk: LightGBM's built-in feature contributions, or, for the GRU, hiding each measurement for the last 12 hours and seeing how much its risk drops.
